title: 'No Kings' Rallies Across the US Urge People to Vote Early
summaryZh: 「No Kings」運動週六全美舉辦數千場活動，呼籲民眾期中選舉提前投票。
summaryHi: "नो किंग्स" आंदोलन ने शनिवार को अमेरिका भर में हज़ारों कार्यक्रम कर लोगों से जल्दी वोट डालने को कहा।
summaryEs: El movimiento "No Kings" celebró miles de actos en EE. UU. para animar a votar por adelantado.
summaryJa: 「ノー・キングス」運動が土曜、全米数千か所で集会を開き、中間選挙の期日前投票を呼びかけた。
summaryKo: '노 킹스' 운동이 토요일 미 전역 수천 곳에서 행사를 열고 중간선거 사전투표를 독려했다.
summaryEn: The "No Kings" movement held thousands of events on Saturday to urge Americans to vote early.
paragraphs: Supporters of the "No Kings" movement held thousands of gatherings across the United States on Saturday, but this time the focus was less on protest and more on the ballot box. The national day of action, called "No Kings: Vote Early", aimed to boost turnout ahead of the midterm elections.

Ezra Levin, co-founder of the progressive group Indivisible, said the movement's first three events had been designed to send a message. "We're done sending a message," he said, explaining that the priority now was getting people to vote.

Events ranged from large marches to block parties and cookouts. In Washington, D.C., crowds gathered at the Lincoln Memorial, while in Golden, Colorado, residents joined a "Paws to the Polls" dog march. In Frisco, Texas, where early voting begins on October 19, volunteers handed out 500 goody bags with QR codes linking to voting resources.
Thousands attended a rally in a Minneapolis park, and around 200 people braved cold, windy weather at the state capitol in Baton Rouge, Louisiana.

Organisers described the effort as nonpartisan, banning political endorsements and inviting no current candidates to speak. Volunteers were also trained as poll watchers. Levin raised concerns about efforts to restrict mail-in voting and about immigration officers being sent to polling places.
On Saturday, people met in thousands of places across the United States. The event was called "No Kings: Vote Early".
The midterm elections are coming soon. The groups behind the event want more people to vote, and to vote early.

There were big marches and small parties. In Washington, D.C., people met at the Lincoln Memorial. In Colorado, people walked with their dogs. In Texas, helpers gave out 500 bags with links to voting information.
In Minneapolis, thousands of people came to a park. In Baton Rouge, about 200 people came, even in cold, windy weather.
The organisers said the event was not for one party. They did not ask any candidates to speak. One leader said: "We're done sending a message." Now, he said, the goal is to get people to vote.

Thousands of events took place across the United States on Saturday as the "No Kings" movement held a national day of action called "No Kings: Vote Early". The aim was to get more people to vote ahead of the midterm elections.

This was different from earlier No Kings protests. Ezra Levin, a co-founder of the group Indivisible, said the first three events were about sending a message. "We're done sending a message," he said. The goal now is to help people vote.

The events were very different in size and style. In Washington, D.C., people rallied at the Lincoln Memorial. In Golden, Colorado, there was a dog march called "Paws to the Polls". In Frisco, Texas, where early voting starts on October 19, organisers gave out 500 bags with QR codes linking to voting information.
Thousands of people joined a rally in a Minneapolis park, while about 200 met at the state capitol in Baton Rouge despite cold, windy weather.
Organisers said the day was nonpartisan. They did not allow political endorsements or invite candidates to speak. Volunteers were also trained to watch polling places.

Supporters of the "No Kings" movement held thousands of gatherings across the United States on Saturday, but this time the focus was less on protest and more on the ballot box. The national day of action, called "No Kings: Vote Early", aimed to boost turnout ahead of the midterm elections.

Ezra Levin, co-founder of the progressive group Indivisible, said the movement's first three events had been designed to send a message. "We're done sending a message," he said, explaining that the priority now was getting people to vote.

Events ranged from large marches to block parties and cookouts. In Washington, D.C., crowds gathered at the Lincoln Memorial, while in Golden, Colorado, residents joined a "Paws to the Polls" dog march. In Frisco, Texas, where early voting begins on October 19, volunteers handed out 500 goody bags with QR codes linking to voting resources.
Thousands attended a rally in a Minneapolis park, and around 200 people braved cold, windy weather at the state capitol in Baton Rouge, Louisiana.

Organisers described the effort as nonpartisan, banning political endorsements and inviting no current candidates to speak. Volunteers were also trained as poll watchers. Levin raised concerns about efforts to restrict mail-in voting and about immigration officers being sent to polling places.

The "No Kings" movement, best known for its mass demonstrations, shifted its emphasis from protest to participation on Saturday, staging thousands of events nationwide under the banner "No Kings: Vote Early" in an effort to drive turnout in the midterm elections.

Ezra Levin, co-founder of the progressive organisation Indivisible, characterised the change bluntly. The first three No Kings events, he said, had been about sending a message: "We're done sending a message." The objective now, he argued, was to translate public anger into votes.

The gatherings varied considerably in scale and tone. Demonstrators assembled at the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, D.C., while Golden, Colorado, hosted a "Paws to the Polls" dog march. In Frisco, Texas, where early voting opens on October 19, volunteers distributed 500 goody bags containing QR codes linked to voting resources.
In Minneapolis, thousands filled a park, whereas roughly 200 people endured bitter, gusty conditions outside the state capitol in Baton Rouge.

Although many signs were openly critical of President Trump, organisers insisted the initiative was nonpartisan, prohibiting endorsements and declining to invite candidates. Volunteers were trained as poll watchers, and Levin voiced concern about attempts to curb mail-in voting and the prospect of immigration officers being stationed at polling places.

In a notable strategic shift, the "No Kings" movement, which previously organised large-scale protests, devoted its latest national day of action to electoral participation. On Saturday, thousands of events took place across the United States under the slogan "No Kings: Vote Early", with the explicit aim of increasing turnout in the midterm elections.

Ezra Levin, co-founder of the progressive group Indivisible, explained the rationale succinctly: earlier events had been intended to send a message, but "We're done sending a message." In his view, the movement's energy should now be channelled into voting.

The format of the events was remarkably diverse. While crowds assembled at the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, D.C., other communities opted for more informal approaches, including a "Paws to the Polls" dog march in Golden, Colorado, and the distribution of 500 goody bags containing QR codes for voting information in Frisco, Texas, where early voting begins on October 19.
Attendance also varied considerably, from thousands in a Minneapolis park to approximately 200 people who withstood cold, windy weather in Baton Rouge.

Organisers emphasised that the initiative was nonpartisan: endorsements were prohibited and no candidates were invited to speak. Nevertheless, concerns about access to the ballot were evident. Volunteers were trained as poll watchers, and Levin criticised efforts to restrict mail-in voting and the possible presence of immigration officers at polling places.

noteEn.meaning: in a short and clear way.

noteHi.exampleTr: उसने एक वाक्य में समस्या संक्षेप में बताई।

noteEs.exampleTr: Ella explicó el problema de forma concisa en una frase.
noteEs.usage: Se usa put it succinctly; adjetivo succinct.

noteJa.exampleTr: 彼女は問題を一文で簡潔に述べた。

noteKo.exampleTr: 그녀는 문제를 한 문장으로 간결하게 말했다.

supporters.en: people who agree with and help an idea
supporters.ex: Supporters of the new park held a meeting.

texas.en: a large US state in the south

there.en: used to say something exists; that place

thousands.en: many thousands; a very large number
thousands.ex: Thousands of birds fly south each year.

time.ex: For the first time, dentists will join.

to.en: towards; also used before a verb

tone.en: the general feeling or style of something
tone.ex: The meeting had a friendly tone.

took.ex: The meeting took place on Monday.

trained.en: taught the skills for a job
trained.ex: She trained as a nurse in London.

translate.en: to change something into another form
translate.ex: It is hard to translate ideas into action.

trump.en: Donald Trump, President of the United States

turnout.en: the number of people who vote or attend
turnout.ex: Turnout was higher than last year.

example.en: Voter turnout was the highest in twenty years.
example.zh: 投票率創二十年來新高。

note.usage: 常見 voter turnout、high/low turnout、boost turnout。

noteEn.meaning: the number of people who vote or attend.

noteHi.exampleTr: मतदान प्रतिशत बीस साल में सबसे ज़्यादा रहा।

noteEs.exampleTr: La participación fue la más alta en veinte años.
noteEs.usage: Se usa voter turnout; high / low turnout.

noteJa.exampleTr: 投票率は20年で最高だった。

under.en: according to a rule or agreement

view.ex: In my view, the plan is too costly.
view.zh: 看法（in their view：在他們看來）

voiced.en: said what you think or feel

volunteers.en: people who work without pay to help

vote.en: a formal choice made by people

votes.ex: The bill won by ten votes.

voting.en: the act of choosing in an election

walked.ex: We walked to the park with our dog.

want.ex: I want a glass of water.

washington.en: the capital city of the United States

weather.ex: The weather in Ireland changes quickly.

where.ex: This is the town where I was born.

which.en: used to add information about a thing

windy.ex: It was too windy to fly the drone.

withstood.en: managed to deal with something hard
withstood.ex: The old bridge withstood the storm.
